title: Week 1A: What Regression Is For
text:
How this course works
Every week has the same rhythm:

Warm-up quiz (10 min): low stakes, checks last week stuck
Mini-lecture, then you analyze data, twice per class
Labs are done in class on your own laptop and count for credit by completion
Homework rewards interpretation, not just running code
One project, four milestones, real public health data of your choice









The deal


I keep the lecturing short. You bring a laptop and actually do regression every single week. By December you will have analyzed data a dozen times, not watched me do it a dozen times.

title: Week 1A: What Regression Is For
text:
AI in this course

You may use AI tools for homework and the project: learning, debugging, drafting
You disclose what you used and for what (one sentence is fine)
You own every word and number you submit: expect to explain any of it
Quizzes and the final exam are in class and AI-free: that is where you prove the understanding is yours


Details in the AI ground rules handout.

title: Week 1A: What Regression Is For
text:
What is a regression question?
All of these are regression questions:

How much does systolic blood pressure rise per decade of age, and does the rate differ between smokers and non-smokers?
Which county characteristics best predict premature death rates, and how well?
After adjusting for age and income, is sleep duration associated with BMI?


Common structure: a continuous outcome y, one or more predictors x, and a question about the relationship.

title: Week 1A: What Regression Is For
section: Three jobs a regression model can do
text:
Three jobs a regression model can do

Description: summarize how y varies with x in these data
Prediction: given a new x, what y should we expect, and how sure are we?
Explanation: what happens to y if x changes? (causal, the hardest)








Warning


Same lm() output, three very different claims. Most regression disasters come from doing job 1 and announcing job 3.

title: Week 1A: What Regression Is For
section: Where it all started: Galton’s heights
text:
Where it all started: Galton’s heights
Francis Galton (1886) collected heights of parents and their adult children.


Code
data("GaltonFamilies")
ggplot(GaltonFamilies, aes(midparentHeight, childHeight)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = 2, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Mid-parent height (in)", y = "Adult child height (in)",
       title = "Galton's families: the original regression")

title: Week 1A: What Regression Is For
text:
Regression to the mean

The fitted line (blue) is flatter than the identity line (red, slope 1)
Tall parents have tall children, but less tall than themselves on average; short parents likewise
Galton called it “regression towards mediocrity”; the name stuck to the whole method


Think-pair-share (2 min): A clinic measures blood pressure twice. Patients flagged as hypertensive at visit 1 tend to look better at visit 2 even with no treatment. Why? What would this do to a naive before-after study of a new drug?

title: Week 1A: What Regression Is For
section: Regression to the mean is everywhere
text:
Regression to the mean is everywhere

The “sophomore slump” and magazine-cover jinx
Speed cameras placed at intersections after crash spikes “work”
Extreme baseline patients improve in single-arm trials


This is why we need control groups and why understanding regression deeply matters for public health practice, not just for fitting lines.

NHANES caveats (say them once, remember all semester)

Our version is a teaching extract: resampled, survey weights ignored
Cross-sectional: one time point per person
Self-reported variables (sleep, alcohol) measured with error


Fine for learning regression; for a real paper you would use the raw NHANES files with survey methods.

title: Course Project
text:
In groups of up to two, you will carry out a complete regression analysis of a public health dataset of your choice: pose a question, explore the data, build and check models, and communicate what you found. The project is worth 30% of the course grade, spread over four milestones so that feedback arrives while it can still help.
AI tools may be used throughout under the course policy (use it, disclose it, own it); the report and presentation each include an AI-use statement.

title: Course Project
text:
Milestone 1: Proposal (1 page)
State your research question, name your dataset (with a link and evidence you can actually load it), identify the continuous outcome and 4+ candidate predictors, and note anything worrying (missing data, small n, odd units).
Rubric (3 pts): feasible dataset in hand, 1; clear continuous-outcome question answerable with linear regression, 1; sensible candidate predictors with units described, 1.
The main purpose is to catch infeasible plans early. You may change course afterward; talk to me first.

title: Course Project
text:
Milestone 2: EDA memo (2-3 pages)
Univariate summaries of outcome and key predictors, at least three informative plots, a missing-data accounting, and a short “what we expect models to show and what might go wrong” paragraph.
Rubric (5 pts): outcome described with appropriate plots/statistics, 1; predictor-outcome relationships explored graphically, 2; missing data and data-quality issues identified honestly, 1; analysis plan updated in light of EDA, 1.

title: Course Project
text:
Milestone 3: Presentation (10 min + 3 min questions)
Both partners speak. Cover: question, data, one EDA highlight, your final model with interpretation, one diagnostic you checked, and one limitation stated plainly. Slides in any tool; submit the file the night before.
Rubric (7 pts): clarity of question and motivation, 1; correctness of statistical content, 2; interpretation precision (the strong-form sentence discipline), 2; diagnostics honestly presented, 1; delivery and timekeeping, 1. Peer feedback forms inform, but do not determine, the delivery point.

title: Course Project
text:
Milestone 4: Final report (max 8 pages + appendix)
Single-spaced, 12 pt, sections: Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion. Unlimited appendix for code and extra output; the 8 pages must stand alone.
Rubric (15 pts):

Introduction (2): question, motivation, data source described
Methods (3): models stated precisely, choices justified (transformations, included variables), inference approach described
Results (6): estimation with interpretation (2), inference (1), diagnostics with consequences addressed (2), model comparison/selection (1)
Discussion (2): findings in context, limitations including confounding
Writing quality and reproducibility (2): report reads cleanly; code in appendix reruns from the raw data

title: Course Project
text:
Picking a dataset
Any public dataset with a continuous outcome and enough observations (n of 200+ recommended) works. Good starting points:

County Health Rankings: county-level health outcomes and factors (countyhealthrankings.org)
NHANES (raw waves, different variables than class): CDC NHANES
BRFSS: state/individual behavioral risk factors (CDC BRFSS)
CDC PLACES: census-tract health estimates (CDC PLACES)
Gapminder / WHO Global Health Observatory: country-level indicators (who.int/data/gho)
EPA Air Quality System: pollution measurements (epa.gov/outdoor-air-quality-data)
NYC Open Data: restaurant inspections, health surveys, vital statistics (opendata.cityofnewyork.us)
IPUMS Health Surveys: harmonized NHIS/MEPS microdata (healthsurveys.ipums.org)
Global Burden of Disease: country-year disease burden (ghdx.healthdata.org)
Tidy Tuesday archives: many curated health-adjacent sets (github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday)

Avoid: time series as your only structure (we do not cover it), binary outcomes (that is Regression II: logistic), and datasets so clean they teach you nothing. A little messiness is a feature; document what you did about it.

How the course works

Hands-on Modeling Studio. Every Tuesday session alternates mini-lectures with guided and open-ended lab exercises, so you actively build and critique models in every class.
Interpretation & AI Critique. Computing models is easy; understanding them is where true expertise lies. Homework assignments emphasize strong-form verbal interpretations and feature dedicated sections where you critique and correct flawed AI-generated statistical reasoning.
Individual Fluency Certification. While AI tools are embraced on homework and projects, short weekly warm-up quizzes and the in-class final exam certify your independent statistical hand-fluency without electronic devices.
Public Health Research Project. You will work in pairs to analyze a real-world public health dataset of your choice, culminating in a conference-style presentation, an AI-use appendix, and a reproducible Quarto report.

Getting started (before Week 1)

Install R (version 4.3+) and RStudio Desktop (both free).
Open RStudio and run in the console:

text: We do all in-class work in R on your own laptop, so the one requirement is arriving at Week 1 with a working setup. Follow these steps and you are done; nothing in this course costs money.

Download and install R from cloud.r-project.org (choose your operating system, accept all defaults). If you already have R, version 4.2 or newer is fine.

title: AI Policy: The Three Zones
text: This course treats AI assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, GitHub Copilot, and similar) as standard tools of modern statistical practice. You will learn to use them effectively and critically, while developing the solid statistical foundation to evaluate and explain models without them.

title: AI Policy: The Three Zones
text:
Why this policy
In professional biostatistics and public health data science, computing models is fast, but judgment, interpretation in context, and diagnostic scrutiny are what protect against false conclusions.
AI tools are prone to subtle statistical errors: 1. Conflating statistical association with causal effects. 2. Fabricating interpretations of adjusted regression coefficients that ignore confounding structures. 3. Overlooking severe residual non-linearity or influential outliers. 4. Hallucinating package syntax, citations, or data definitions.
Banning AI tools would fail to prepare you for modern practice; relying on them blindly would leave you unable to catch their errors. This course trains you to direct AI tools purposefully, verify their mathematical and contextual accuracy, and take full ownership of your statistical work.

title: AI Policy: The Three Zones
text:
Requirements & Ethics

Free-tier tools are sufficient: All coursework can be completed with free-tier AI assistants; no paid subscriptions are required or expected.
Ownership: “The AI told me to” is never an acceptable defense for an erroneous model, an incorrect interpretation, or broken code.
Integrity: Submitting AI-generated analyses you cannot explain, using AI during quizzes or exams, or omitting required disclosures constitutes an academic integrity violation.

title: AI Ground Rules
text: AI assistants are part of how statistics gets done now. Banning them would teach you nothing about using them well, and “using them well” is a skill your employers will expect. So here is the deal.

title: AI Ground Rules
text:
The three rules
1. Use it. On homework and the project you may use AI tools (ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, or similar) to learn concepts, debug code, explore approaches, and improve writing. Some homework problems will hand you AI output and require you to critique it.
2. Disclose it. Every homework and project submission ends with a one- or two-sentence AI-use statement. Examples:

“I used Claude to debug a ggplot error in Q2 and to suggest wording for my Q4 interpretation, which I revised.”


“No AI tools used.”

Honest disclosure is never penalized. Missing or false disclosure is an academic integrity violation.
3. Own it. You are responsible for every word and number you submit. “The AI said so” does not excuse a wrong answer, an invented reference, or code you cannot explain. I may ask you to walk me through any part of your submission, and the weekly quizzes and final exam (both in class, no AI) check that the understanding is actually yours.

title: AI Ground Rules
text:
What good use looks like

“Explain why my residual plot fans out and what that violates” then reading the cited textbook section to confirm
Pasting an error message and asking for the bug, then understanding the fix before moving on
Drafting an interpretation yourself, asking AI to critique it, keeping your own voice

title: AI Ground Rules
section: What weak use looks like (allowed, but it will cost you)
text:
What weak use looks like (allowed, but it will cost you)

Pasting the whole homework in and copying answers out. The interpretation questions are graded on precision and context; generic AI prose scores poorly, and quiz day always comes.
Submitting code you cannot explain. It shows immediately when I ask.

title: AI Ground Rules
section: Why the quizzes and exam are AI-free
text:
Why the quizzes and exam are AI-free
Not distrust; calibration. You need regular, honest evidence of what you can do unaided, and so do I. Think of AI-free checkpoints as the treadmill stress test and AI-assisted work as daily life with your fitness tracker on.

title: Course Project: Public Health Regression Study
text:
In groups of up to two, you will carry out an end-to-end regression analysis of a real-world public health dataset of your choice: pose an impactful health question, explore and clean the data, formulate and refine multiple regression models, run diagnostic checks, and communicate your findings in both an oral presentation and a written manuscript.
The project is worth 30% of the course grade, spread across four milestones so that feedback arrives while it can still shape your analysis.
AI tools may be used throughout under the course AI policy (verify-then-use with explicit disclosure).

title: Course Project: Public Health Regression Study
text:
Milestone 1: Proposal (1 page, 3%)
State your research question, name your public health data source (with a direct link and proof of loadability), identify your continuous outcome and at least 4 candidate predictors (with units), and note any initial data challenges (missingness, sample size, skewness).
Rubric (3 pts): - Feasible dataset in hand (1 pt) - Clear continuous-outcome question suitable for linear regression (1 pt) - Sensible candidate predictors with units described (1 pt)

title: Course Project: Public Health Regression Study
text:
Milestone 2: EDA Memo (2–3 pages, 5%)
Provide univariate distributions of outcome and key predictors, at least three informative bivariate plots (with smooths/faceting), an honest accounting of missing data, and a summary of expected modeling relationships and anticipated challenges (non-linearity, collinearity, outliers).
Rubric (5 pts): - Outcome described with plots and summary statistics (1 pt) - Predictor-outcome relationships explored graphically (2 pts) - Missing data and data quality issues addressed honestly (1 pt) - Modeling plan updated in light of exploratory findings (1 pt)

title: Course Project: Public Health Regression Study
text:
Milestone 3: Presentation (10 min + 3 min Q&A, 7%)
Both partners must speak. Your presentation should cover: 1. Research question and public health motivation (1 slide). 2. Data source and one key EDA finding. 3. Your primary fitted multiple regression model with strong-form coefficient interpretations. 4. One diagnostic test/plot you investigated and how you resolved or acknowledged it. 5. Key limitations and implications.

text:
Recommended Public Health Datasets
Any publicly available dataset with a continuous outcome and sufficient sample size (n \ge 200) is eligible:

County Health Rankings: County-level health outcomes, clinical care, and socioeconomic factors (countyhealthrankings.org)
CDC NHANES: Continuous national survey on nutrition and metabolic health (wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes)
CDC BRFSS: Behavioral risk factors and chronic disease surveillance (cdc.gov/brfss)
CDC PLACES: Census-tract and local health outcome estimates (cdc.gov/places)
WHO Global Health Observatory: Cross-country health and life-expectancy metrics (who.int/data/gho)
EPA Outdoor Air Quality Data: Environmental exposures and particulate matter (epa.gov/outdoor-air-quality-data)
NYC Open Data: Citywide community health surveys, air quality, and vital statistics (opendata.cityofnewyork.us)
IPUMS Health Surveys: Harmonized NHIS and MEPS microdata (healthsurveys.ipums.org)
Global Burden of Disease (GBD): Disability-adjusted life years and disease burden (ghdx.healthdata.org)
TidyTuesday Health Archives: Curated public health and epidemiological datasets (github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday)

title: Syllabus
text:
Course Description
Regression models are one of the most important statistical techniques used in public health. This course focuses on data analysis that uses linear regression models for continuous outcomes. The first part of this course introduces simple and multiple linear regressions, principles of ordinary least square regression models, model assumptions, and inferences about model parameters. The second part of the course focuses on important practical matters, such as prediction, diagnostics, and variable selection. These two parts together provide the foundations for more advanced statistical modeling. Examples are drawn from broad areas of public health research. All the analyses will be taught and performed using R statistical software.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course Overview
This course emphasizes modern, reproducible, and active statistical practice in public health. Class sessions follow a hands-on studio rhythm: short conceptual mini-lectures alternate with guided data analyses and paired coding labs in RStudio using real-world health datasets (including NHANES, US county health metrics, and clinical trials). All computational work is done using R and Quarto. In addition, an integrated “AI Policy & Practice” component trains students to use modern AI assistants productively and defensively for exploratory coding while developing the rigorous statistical judgment required to verify, interpret, and critique quantitative outputs.

The correlation is real

[1] 0.8006078

Published in NEJM (tongue in cheek… mostly)

title: Week 1B: Association Is Not Causation
text:
Confounding

A confounder is a third variable driving both x and y
Here: national wealth buys both chocolate and research universities



Code
ggplot(chocolate, aes(INTERNET, NOBEL)) +
  geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Internet penetration (%)", y = "Nobel laureates per 10M",
       title = "Internet access 'predicts' Nobel prizes too")

title: Week 1B: Association Is Not Causation
section: Association vs causation: the honest hierarchy
text:
Association vs causation: the honest hierarchy

Association: y tends to be higher when x is higher (regression can show this)
Adjusted association: …even after holding measured confounders fixed (regression can show this, if you measured the right things)
Causation: changing x would change y (needs design: randomization, natural experiments, or strong assumptions)


Regression is our tool for 1 and 2. Claiming 3 requires arguments outside the model. We will practice writing sentences that claim exactly as much as the analysis supports.

title: Week 1B: Association Is Not Causation
text:
The linear model, formally
For an outcome y and predictor x:
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad i = 1, \ldots, n

\beta_0: intercept, the mean of y when x = 0
\beta_1: slope, the difference in mean y per one-unit difference in x
\varepsilon_i: error, everything about y_i the line does not capture


Next week: how to find the best \beta_0, \beta_1 and what “best” even means.
